  <section class="case-study__section">
    <h2>The question</h2>
    <p>The headline number — DFW rate from 39% to under 5% — is the kind of stat that sounds too clean to be true. So the question I cared about wasn't <em>"did the rate drop?"</em>. It was the harder one: <em>did it drop for the students it most needed to drop for, did it hold across instructors and semesters, and what would have happened to those students under the old design?</em></p>
    <p>A pass rate that improves on average can hide a redesign that helped students who would have passed anyway. That's the version of "success" I wanted to rule out.</p>
  </section>

      <li>Per-student outcome data (final grade, withdrawal, persistence into the next required course in the major).</li>
      <li>Demographic and academic-history fields available through the institutional data office, used for stratified analysis where sample sizes allowed.</li>
      <li>Embedded formative-assessment data from the asynchronous content library — which questions students missed, where they got stuck, and how that mapped to downstream exam performance.</li>
    </ul>
    <p>All identifying data was handled through the institutional research office under standard educational data protections. The analysis below is reconstructed from de-identified summaries and is presented at the level of group-level outcomes only.</p>

    <p>The short version of the takeaway, written in the voice I'd use for a real report:</p>

    <div class="pull-quote">The redesign didn't pull up the average by helping students who would have passed anyway. It moved the bottom of the distribution. The students whose outcomes changed most were the ones the old design was already failing.</div>

  <section class="case-study__section">
    <h2>What I'd dig into next</h2>
    <p>A clean case study is honest about what it didn't answer. A few open questions I'd want time on:</p>
    <ul>
      <li><strong>Causal attribution.</strong> Pre/post is a defensible design at the section level, but it isn't a randomized comparison. A staggered-rollout or matched-section analysis, where feasible, would tighten the causal claim.</li>
      <li><strong>Long-tail equity.</strong> The headline gaps closed, but small-sample subgroups deserve their own look once enough cohorts have accrued. I'd want to be careful about under-powered claims of equivalence.</li>
      <li><strong>Item-bank fairness.</strong> With formative assessment data this rich, it's worth running differential item functioning analyses on the question bank itself. A redesign that closes the gap on outcomes but uses biased items is still doing harm.</li>
    </ul>
  </section>
